claims.text: Surface segregation of low-melting-point elements controls the onset of premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface segregation of low-melting-point elements reduces the overall melting temperature of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The reduction in melting temperature results from weakened surface lattice cohesion.
The as-synthesized 5–20 nm HEA nanoparticles are random solid solutions.
Subsolidus annealing will enrich the nanoparticle surface in the constituent element having the lowest melting point.
Quenching the control batch will retain a uniform composition.
The surface concentration profile of the lowest-melting-point element is the structural mediator linking thermal history to melting behavior.
Segregated surface sites have reduced atomic coordination.
Segregated surface sites have weaker bonding.
Reduced coordination and weaker bonding at segregated surface sites initiate premelting at lower temperatures.
Premelting initiated at the segregated surface propagates inward.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will begin surface premelting 50–100 K below the uniform-composition baseline.
Annealed, surface-segregated nanoparticles will undergo bulk melting 50–100 K below the uniform-composition baseline.
The proposed relationship holds for 5–20 nm HEA nanoparticles whose constituent-element melting points differ by at least 200 K under inert or vacuum conditions.
Kinetic barriers to segregation and measurement precision may shift the observed melting-temperature difference by approximately ±20 K.
The comparison will use annealing at approximately 0.7 times the mixture melting temperature for the segregation treatment.
A difference of less than 20 K between annealed and quenched batches in premelting onset or melting temperature will falsify the hypothesis.
